## Introduction

This analysis uses the [Our World in Data-Energy](https://github.com/owid/energy-data) published by University of Oxford. This dataset contains 130 variables across 220 countries from year 1900 to 2025. It covers country-level data on energy use and electricity generation. I look at how energy use relates to income and how much electricity comes from clean and fossil sources respectively, because cleaner electricity is an important part of climate policy.

## Data Preparation

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(readr)
owid_energy_data <- read_csv("data/owid-energy-data.csv")
```

```{r}
# Keep only countries (rows without an ISO code are regions like "World" or "Europe")
countries <- owid_energy_data |>
  filter(!is.na(iso_code))

# Five large countries to compare
my_countries <- c("Brazil", "China", "Germany", "India", "United States")
```

## Graph 1: Income and Energy Use

```{r}
countries |>
  filter(year == 2022) |>
  mutate(gdp_per_capita = gdp / population) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdp_per_capita, y = energy_per_capita)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = population), alpha = 0.5, color = "blue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "orange") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Richer countries use more energy per person",
       subtitle = "GDP per capita and energy use per capita, 2022",
       x = "GDP per capita (international-$, log scale)",
       y = "Energy per capita (Kwh, log scale)",
       size = "Population",
       caption = "Source: Our World in Data Energy Dataset") +
    theme_minimal()
```

#### Each point in this graph is a country, and the size of the point shows its population. Countries with higher GDP per capita use much more energy per person, and most points stay close to the trend line. This means that as poorer countries grow richer, their energy use is likely to rise. 

## Graph 2: Renewable Electricity Overtime

```{r}
countries |>
  filter(country %in% my_countries, year >= 2000, year <= 2024) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = renewables_share_elec, color = country, linetype = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 2) +
  labs(title = "German had the biggest increase in renewable electricity",
       subtitle = "Share of electricity from renewables in five countries, 2000-2024",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Share of electricity from renewables (%)",
       color = "Country",
       linetype = "Country",
       caption = "Source: Our World in Data Energy Dataset") +
  theme_minimal()
```

#### Germany’s renewable share rose from about 6% in 2000 to about 59% in 2024. China and the United States also grew, but more slowly, and India grew the least. Brazil was already near 90% the whole time because it uses a lot of hydropower.

## Graph 3: Fossil Fuels in Electricity

```{r}
countries |>
  filter(country %in% my_countries, year == 2024) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = country, y = fossil_share_elec, fill = country)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  labs(
    title = "India relies most on fossil fuels for electricity",
    subtitle = "Share of electricity from coal, oil and gas, 2024",
    x = "Country",
    y = "Share of electricity from fossil fuels (%)",
    fill = "Country",
    caption = "Source: Our World in Data Energy Dataset"
  ) + 
  theme_minimal()
```

#### In 2024, fossil fuels made about 78% of India’s electricity and about 62% of China’s, but only about 11% of Brazil’s. Countries that still depend heavily on fossil fuels have the most room to cut emissions.

## Graph 4: Improved Version of Graph 2

I want to improve my graph 2 using Gemini. My prompt for Gemini: I've created this graph using ggplot2 to compare the share of renewable electricity in five countries: China, Brazil, German, India, and United States from 2000-2024. The data set I used is Our Word in Data-Energy. Now I want you to improve this image, polish it and give me some coding suggestions.

![](images/83a15bfa5000f26451deba140e2c77cb.png){width="1258"}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 6.8
#| out-width: "100%"   
#| fig-align: "center"  

library(tidyverse)
library(scales)

# 1. Load data and filter relevant countries (2000-2024)
owid_data <- read.csv("data/owid-energy-data.csv")

countries_of_interest <- c("Brazil", "China", "Germany", "India", "United States")

df_filtered <- owid_data %>%
  filter(country %in% countries_of_interest, year >= 2000, year <= 2024) %>%
  select(country, year, renewables_share_elec) %>%
  drop_na()

# 2. Extract endpoints for direct line labeling
df_endpoints <- df_filtered %>%
  filter(year == 2024) %>%
  mutate(label = paste0(country, " (", round(renewables_share_elec), "%)"))

# Baseline 2000 start point for Germany
df_germany_2000 <- df_filtered %>%
  filter(country == "Germany", year == 2000)

# 3. Custom color palette and line widths
country_colors <- c(
  "Germany"       = "#00875A", # Vibrant highlight green
  "Brazil"        = "#0052CC", # Deep navy
  "China"         = "#DE350B", # Vermilion red
  "United States" = "#FFAB00", # Warm amber
  "India"         = "#6B778C"  # Slate grey
)

country_sizes <- c(
  "Germany"       = 1.5,
  "Brazil"        = 0.9,
  "China"         = 0.9,
  "United States" = 0.9,
  "India"         = 0.9
)

# 4. Build ggplot graph
p <- ggplot(df_filtered, aes(x = year, y = renewables_share_elec, color = country, group = country)) +
  # Lines with variable thickness
  geom_line(aes(size = country), lineend = "round") +
  scale_size_manual(values = country_sizes, guide = "none") +
  scale_color_manual(values = country_colors, guide = "none") +
  
  # Terminal points at 2024 and Germany 2000 start
  geom_point(data = df_endpoints, aes(x = year, y = renewables_share_elec), size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(data = df_germany_2000, aes(x = year, y = renewables_share_elec), color = "#00875A", size = 2.5) +
  
  # Direct end-of-line text labels
  geom_text(
    data = df_endpoints,
    aes(label = label),
    hjust = -0.15,
    fontface = if_else(df_endpoints$country == "Germany", "bold", "plain"),
    size = 3.8,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  
  # Scale and axis limits
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2024),
    limits = c(2000, 2029),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = percent_format(scale = 1),
    limits = c(0, 100),
    breaks = seq(0, 100, 25)
  ) +
  
  # Titles and captions
  labs(
    title = "Germany Led Renewable Growth with a 50+ Percentage-Point Surge",
    subtitle = "Share of electricity generation from renewable sources (2000–2024)",
    caption = "Source: Our World in Data Energy Dataset (2024)",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  
  # Clean minimal theme
  theme_minimal()
print(p)
```
